segments.line: The app on your phone says thirty- nine point two.
You were standing at the counter. Now you're on your knees, and you didn't decide to kneel.
Here's what's happening inside you. Your heart pumps blood up to your brain, about thirty centimeters uphill.
Now that blood weighs four times as much, and your heart was never built for that.
Fighter pilots know this feeling. When they turn hard, they feel the same pull. Without help, their vision goes gray at about three to four g.
Then it goes dark. Then they pass out. That's real.
And you're at four g, standing in your kitchen.
So you do the only thing that helps. You lie down. Flat on your back.
Now your blood doesn't have to climb. Your brain gets it back. The gray clears.
Across the whole planet, eight billion people do the same thing. They lie down wherever they are. On sidewalks, in offices, in the middle of the road. The
trained pilots in G- suits? They can handle eight or nine g. But only for seconds, in a jet, with a special suit squeezing their legs.
Nobody has ever done it for an hour.
And outside, things start to break. A tree in the yard groans, and a branch rips off. Gutters fold.
Shelves in the kitchen snap and the plates come down like bullets.
Biscuit crawls across the floor on his belly and lies down next to you. He's shaking. You do
the math. In one hour, it's eight g. In two hours, sixteen.
And nobody, anywhere, knows how to survive sixteen.
